summary: Describes the BGP Large Communities attribute, an extension that signals opaque information within separate namespaces to help routing management, usable with four-octet ASNs.

eli5.summary: Sticky notes on routes that tell other networks how to treat them, with room for big network numbers.

questions: how big is a bgp large community
what is the large community attribute type code
how are bgp large communities written
subtitle: A 12-byte BGP community tag that fits four-byte AS numbers, so every network can label routes without collisions.

tldr.problem: The classic BGP Communities value is 32 bits, split into two 16-bit halves, so it cannot hold a four-octet ASN. Extended Communities are six octets, still too small for the common practice of putting a four-octet ASN in both administrator fields.
tldr.mechanism: The Large Communities attribute carries one or more 12-octet values: a four-octet Global Administrator (normally an ASN) and two four-octet operator-defined fields.
tldr.outcome: Operators of any AS, including four-octet ones, can tag routes with their own policy values without collisions. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8092 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the BGP Large Communities attribute.

sections.title: Why Communities Needed to Grow
sections.content:
Network operators attach BGP communities to routes to associate properties with them, such as where the route originated or a routing policy action to take. Because communities are optional transitive attributes, other Autonomous Systems (ASes) on the Internet may act on them in their own routing policies.

The original RFC 1997 attribute is a set of four-octet values. Common use splits each value into two 16-bit words: the top word is an ASN and the bottom word is a value the AS owner defines. Once four-octet ASNs arrived (RFC 6793), a two-octet word could no longer hold the ASN. The Extended Communities attribute (RFC 4360) has a six-octet value, which also cannot hold a four-octet ASN in both its Global Administrator and Local Administrator sub-fields.
sections.eli5: The old label had two small boxes, and a big network number would not fit in the first one. So a new, roomier label was needed.

sections.title: The Large Community Value
sections.content:
Large Communities is an optional transitive path attribute of variable length. All routes carrying it belong to the communities it lists. Each value is a 12-octet quantity made of three 32-bit fields: Global Administrator (a namespace identifier), Local Data Part 1 and Local Data Part 2 (both operator-defined).

The Global Administrator field exists so different ASes can define communities without collision. It SHOULD be an ASN, and then the owner of that ASN decides what the two local parts mean. Using reserved ASNs (0, 65535 and 4294967295) is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The label has three number slots. The first says whose label it is, and the other two are free for that network to use however it likes.

sections.title: Ordering, Duplicates and Aggregation
sections.content:
The order of the 12-octet values inside the attribute has no significance, and a speaker can transmit them in any order. Duplicate values MUST NOT be transmitted, and a receiving speaker MUST silently remove redundant duplicates.

When a range of routes is aggregated, the aggregate should carry a Large Communities attribute containing all the Large Communities from all the aggregated routes.
sections.eli5: It does not matter what order the labels are in, and a repeated label is just thrown away. If routes are bundled together, the bundle keeps everyone's labels.

sections.title: Canonical Text Representation
sections.content:
The canonical way to write a Large Community is three unsigned decimal integers in the order Global Administrator, Local Data 1, Local Data 2, separated by single colons. Numbers MUST NOT have leading zeros, and zero is written as a single 0. Examples from the RFC are 64496:4294967295:2 and 64496:0:0.

Large Communities SHOULD be represented in this canonical form.
sections.eli5: Everyone writes the three numbers the same way, with colons between them, so people can read each other's labels.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
An attribute is malformed if its length in octets is not a non-zero multiple of 12. Duplicate values do not make it malformed. A BGP UPDATE message with a malformed Large Communities attribute is handled with treat-as-withdraw, as described in Section 2 of RFC 7606.

The Global Administrator field may hold any value. An attribute MUST NOT be considered malformed because that field has an unallocated, unassigned or reserved ASN.
sections.eli5: If a label is cut off and does not have complete groups of three numbers, the route in that message is treated as taken back. Odd-looking owner numbers are fine though.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not change security issues of other BGP community mechanisms. An AS that relies on Large Communities must trust every other AS in the path, because any intermediate AS may have added, deleted or altered the attribute. Large Communities do not protect the integrity of each value, and providing such protection is part of the broader task of securing BGP, which is out of scope. Administrators should note Section 11 of RFC 7454.
sections.eli5: Any network along the way can change the labels, so you have to trust the networks in between.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned path attribute type value 32, named LARGE_COMMUNITY, in the BGP Path Attributes subregistry of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Parameters registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of label types now has an entry, number 32, for this new kind of label.

fields.name: Global Administrator
fields.desc: A four-octet namespace identifier, normally an ASN.
